Using the weights downstream: which analysis for which question

Recipes for outcome comparisons, censored data, predictors, and rank tests

Source: vignettes/downstream-analysis.Rmd
downstream-analysis.Rmd

Read vignette("measurement-error") first for what τ2\tau^2, viv_i, the weight and the reliability mean. This page is organised by what you want to do.

Pick the recipe

You want to… Noisy variable is the… Use
Compare groups or time points outcome meta-regression with v_meas (recommended), or brms
Compare groups when some samples are below/above the curve outcome, censored censored model or rank test
Relate antibody to infection, or one antigen to another predictor regression calibration
Report how correlated two assays really are both disattenuation
Compare two groups without a model outcome rank test

Three rules apply to every recipe.

  1. Subset first, then normalise. Weights are scaled to mean 1 over the rows they were computed on. After you filter to one arm or one time point, call normalize_weights() on the rows you actually analyse.
  2. Do not weight censored samples. Represent them by their limit (censor_type, bound), not by w.
  3. Pass the right variance to the right function. Software that estimates τ2\tau^2 itself (metafor) needs the measurement variance v_meas. Software that expects a weight (lm(weights =), brms) needs w_norm. Passing the total variance to metafor would count τ2\tau^2 twice.

A small data set

The examples below simulate what the weight table looks like for 150 people in two arms, each sampled at two visits, so everything runs without a database. In practice the table comes from I-SPI (Weights tab, Data tab download) or from fit_precision_weights(model = "additive") followed by join_weights().

set.seed(11)
n_pat <- 150
d <- data.frame(patient = rep(seq_len(n_pat), each = 2),
                arm     = rep(c("A", "B"), each = n_pat))
d$obs <- seq_len(nrow(d))
tau <- 0.4
b_pat <- rnorm(n_pat, 0, tau)
true  <- 1 + 0.30 * (d$arm == "B") + b_pat[d$patient]
d$se_meas <- exp(rnorm(nrow(d), log(0.2), 0.8))        # curve SE per sample
d$yi      <- true + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, d$se_meas)       # observed log10 value
d$censor_type <- "none"

d <- compute_additive_weights(d, tau2 = tau^2 + 0.0, kappa = 1,
                              censor_col = "censor_type")
head(d[, c("patient", "arm", "yi", "se_meas", "v_meas", "w", "w_norm", "reliability")], 4)
#>   patient arm        yi    se_meas      v_meas        w    w_norm reliability
#> 1       1   A 0.6873140 0.05578947 0.003112464 6.130739 1.3644421   0.9809183
#> 2       1   A 1.3692189 0.34212506 0.117049557 3.609463 0.8033130   0.5775140
#> 3       2   A 0.6939739 0.28115219 0.079046557 4.183286 0.9310217   0.6693257
#> 4       2   A 1.6282186 0.34723252 0.120570420 3.564168 0.7932323   0.5702668

Recipe 1: meta-regression with metafor

metafor::rma.mv() is the cleanest tool when the outcome is noisy and each observation has a known measurement variance. It estimates the extra variance (between samples τ2\tau^2; between patients) by REML and applies the correct weights, so you supply only the measurement variance.

library(metafor)
#> Loading required package: Matrix
#> Loading required package: metadat
#> Loading required package: numDeriv
#> 
#> Loading the 'metafor' package (version 5.2-1). For an
#> introduction to the package please type: help(metafor)
fit <- rma.mv(yi = yi, V = meas_variance(d), mods = ~ arm,
              random = list(~ 1 | patient, ~ 1 | obs),
              data = d, method = "REML")
round(coef(summary(fit)), 3)
#>         estimate    se   zval pval ci.lb ci.ub
#> intrcpt    0.964 0.044 21.899    0 0.878 1.050
#> armB       0.336 0.062  5.393    0 0.214 0.458
  • V = meas_variance(d) is viv_i (measurement only).
  • ~ 1 | obs (one level per row) is the between-sample variance, the model’s τ2\tau^2; ~ 1 | patient is a patient-level variance for repeated measures.
  • The coefficient armB is the group difference on the log10 scale. Multiply 10estimate10^{\text{estimate}} for a fold change.

Compare with ordinary least squares ignoring the weights:

fit_ols <- lm(yi ~ arm, data = d)
round(coef(summary(fit_ols)), 3)
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept)    0.964      0.043  22.627        0
#> armB           0.350      0.060   5.813        0

Both estimate the same difference; the weighted analysis is generally the more precise one, and it does not let a few very well-measured samples drive the answer because their weight is capped at 1/τ21/\tau^2.

Do not use method = "FE" with these weights. Older documentation advised that for the multiplicative model; it assumes there is no between-sample variance beyond the assay error, which is rarely true for people.

Recipe 2: brms, censored outcomes, repeated measures

brms fits the full model and lets censored samples contribute through their limits. The same structure the weights come from:

library(brms)
d_q <- d[d$censor_type == "none", ]          # quantified rows get weights
d_q$w_norm <- normalize_weights(d_q)$w_norm  # re-normalise on the analysis subset

# 1. quantified-only, weighted:
f1 <- brm(yi | weights(w_norm) ~ arm + (1 | patient), data = d_q)

# 2. all rows, with censoring and measurement-error SDs (preferred):
#    d_cens is the output of prepare_censoring(); cens_flag is 0 quantified,
#    -1 left, 1 right, 2 interval. Not run here (needs Stan).
f2 <- brm(bf(yi | cens(cens_flag, yi2) ~ arm + (1 | patient),
             nlf(sigma ~ log(sqrt(exp(2 * ltau) + se_meas^2))),
             ltau ~ 1),
          data = d_cens)

Model 2 matches the additive likelihood: total SD τ2+se2\sqrt{\tau^2 + se^2}, with censored rows contributing probabilities. Use it when more than a few percent of your samples are out of range.

Recipe 3: when the noisy variable is a predictor

Weights cannot fix this. Suppose you regress an immune outcome on antibody level: noise in the antibody level pulls the slope towards zero.

set.seed(5)
n  <- 3000
x  <- rnorm(n, 0, 0.4)                              # true level (log10)
se <- exp(rnorm(n, log(0.25), 0.5))
x_obs <- x + rnorm(n, 0, se)                        # measured level
y  <- 1.0 * x + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)                    # true slope = 1

p <- data.frame(se_meas = se, x_obs = x_obs, cell = "all")
p <- compute_additive_weights(p, tau2 = 0.4^2, kappa = 1)
x_cal <- reliability_correct(p$x_obs, p$cell, p$reliability)

c(true      = 1,
  naive     = unname(coef(lm(y ~ x_obs))[2]),
  corrected = unname(coef(lm(y ~ x_cal))[2]))
#>      true     naive corrected 
#> 1.0000000 0.6014975 0.9842421

The naive slope is biased toward 0 by roughly the mean reliability; regression calibration (reliability_correct()) recovers the true value. For publication, note two caveats: standard errors from the second stage ignore the uncertainty in the calibration step (bootstrap it, or use brms::me() for a single joint model), and the correction assumes the measurement error is independent of the outcome.

For a correlation between two assays (for example IgG1 to PT versus IgG1 to FHA) use attenuation_correct():

attenuation_correct(r = 0.42, rel_x = p$reliability, rel_y = p$reliability)
#> [1] 0.6127692

Report the observed correlation and the corrected one together; a corrected correlation above 1 in absolute value means the reliabilities are too optimistic or the sample is small, and the function warns.

Recipe 4: rank tests with censored data

If you prefer not to assume a distribution, the censoring-aware rank tests come from survival analysis, where censored observations are the norm. For left-censored assay data, flip the sign so the censoring becomes right censoring, then use a log-rank-type test with Peto-Peto (Prentice-Wilcoxon) weights, rho = 1, a close relative of the Gehan test that weights early differences more:

library(survival)
set.seed(8)
r <- data.frame(arm = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 120))
r$y     <- rnorm(240, 1 + 0.4 * (r$arm == "B"), 0.5)
lod     <- 0.7                                       # lower limit, log10
r$cens  <- r$y < lod                                  # below the limit
r$y_use <- ifelse(r$cens, lod, r$y)                   # replace by the limit
M <- max(r$y_use) + 1
r$t     <- M - r$y_use                                # flip: left becomes right
r$event <- as.integer(!r$cens)                        # 1 = quantified (observed)
survdiff(Surv(t, event) ~ arm, data = r, rho = 1)
#> Call:
#> survdiff(formula = Surv(t, event) ~ arm, data = r, rho = 1)
#> 
#>         N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
#> arm=A 120     42.7     69.8      10.5      38.3
#> arm=B 120     72.9     45.8      16.0      38.3
#> 
#>  Chisq= 38.3  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 6e-10

This replaces the older advice of survey::svyranktest() with weights: that function treats the weights as sampling weights and ignores censoring entirely. A rank test does not use w at all; it makes no use of the measurement-error information, which makes it a useful sensitivity check for the model-based results above.

Checklist before you publish

  • State the model used (model column) and the curveRweights version (weights_pkg_version).
  • State how many samples were censored (n_censored) and how they were handled.
  • Report group reliabilities; if they are below roughly 0.5 say that individual values are not reliable.
  • Run one sensitivity analysis that uses no weights, and one that uses a different censoring treatment (rank test or Tobit); conclusions should agree.
  • Do not mix weights from different runs in one analysis: the stored weight set for a sample is replaced by the most recent run.

References

  • Viechtbauer W. Conducting meta-analyses in R with the metafor package. J Stat Softw 2010;36(3).
  • Bürkner P-C. brms: An R package for Bayesian multilevel models using Stan. J Stat Softw 2017;80(1).
  • Peto R, Peto J. Asymptotically efficient rank invariant test procedures. J R Stat Soc A 1972;135:185-207.
  • Rosner B, Spiegelman D, Willett WC. Correction of logistic regression relative risk estimates and confidence intervals for measurement error. Am J Epidemiol 1990;132:734-45. (Regression calibration.)
  • Hughes MD. Analysis and design issues for studies using censored biomarker measurements. Biometrics 2000;56:445-52.
